section_summary: This final section combines routine export-control correspondence with reports on strategic materials, including reclaimed rubber, coal-hydrogenation products, Bolivian ores, and Canadian nickel shipments to Japan. Most of the section concerns demands by Bishop James Cannon Jr. and members of the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression for a U.S. embargo on scrap iron, petroleum, metals, machinery, and other supplies sustaining Japan’s war in China. It also includes the State Department’s explanation of the limits of the Neutrality Act and Ralph L. Harding’s detailed economic and strategic argument for ending American material support of Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Joosten & Janssen concerning scrap and reclaimed rubber
subfiles.about: Clarifies that scrap rubber and reclaimed rubber fall within the government’s policy on exports of strategic and critical raw materials.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges the firm’s April 11 inquiry and confirms that both scrap and reclaimed rubber are covered by the existing strategic-materials export policy. Copies of two Army and Navy Munitions Board releases explaining the policy are enclosed.

subfiles.title: Charles O. Brown on coal-hydrogenation products and aviation fuel
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Explains how the output of a proposed coal-hydrogenation plant would support aviation-fuel and lubricant production.
subfiles.summary: Brown clarifies that coal-hydrogenation products cannot be converted directly and economically into aviation gasoline. He argues, however, that the proposed plant would supply aviation lubricants and oils that would free lighter motor fuels for refining into aviation gasoline.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese purchases of Bolivian tin and other ores
subfiles.about: References a despatch reporting arrangements for Japanese purchases of Bolivian tin ore and other minerals.
subfiles.summary: The note points to Despatch No. 135 concerning mineral purchases for shipment to Japan through Banco Minero. The bank’s manager reportedly stated that the Japanese were paying in full through the Grace National Bank and National City Bank in New York.

subfiles.title: Treasury Department transmittal to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Apparently transmits the following Treasury correspondence concerning nickel shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The surviving OCR identifies a Treasury Department communication addressed to Secretary of State Cordell Hull but leaves most of its text illegible. A State Department receipt stamp dated March 21, 1940, and its position before the March 20 letter indicate that it served as a cover or transmittal for that document.

subfiles.title: Secretary of the Treasury to President Roosevelt on Canadian nickel shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports a temporary Canadian postponement of further nickel contracts with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The writer reports that International Nickel of Canada’s remaining 835 tons under a 1939 Japanese contract had been spread over January through March rather than shipped in the shorter period Japan requested. Purvis advised that the Canadian government had postponed further nickel contracts and had notified the Japanese minister in Ottawa. The writer considers this evidence that the Allied Purchasing Mission was cooperating with the United States.

subfiles.title: White House referral of correspondence to the State Department
subfiles.from: Stephen Early, Secretary to the President
subfiles.about: Refers the accompanying presidential correspondence to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Stephen Early respectfully refers the attached material to the State Department. The note served as the White House routing sheet for Bishop James Cannon Jr.’s appeal to the President.

subfiles.title: Bishop James Cannon Jr. to President Roosevelt urging an embargo against Japan
subfiles.about: Urges Roosevelt to end American trade supporting Japan’s war against China and to seek congressional embargo legislation.
subfiles.summary: Cannon reviews his unanswered or ineffectual appeals since 1937 for action against Japanese aggression in China and argues that Japan has violated the Kellogg Pact and Nine-Power Treaty. He criticizes Roosevelt’s failure to declare that a state of war exists and contrasts U.S. peace efforts in Europe with its policy in East Asia. Citing Madame Chiang Kai-shek, he contends that American money, scrap iron, vehicles, oil, and other supplies sustain Japan’s campaign. He asks Roosevelt to champion legislation ending what he calls the United States’ practical partnership with Japan.

subfiles.title: An Open Letter to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Publishes Cannon’s appeal for an end to American material assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: This is a printed or separately typed version of Cannon’s letter, repeating his indictment of Japanese aggression and his criticism of American inaction. It argues that invocation of neutrality legislation and an embargo would help end the war in China without requiring U.S. entry into war. Cannon appeals for congressional measures stopping supplies and financial support to Japan.

subfiles.title: R. Walton Moore’s reply to Bishop James Cannon Jr.
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Cannon’s views and explains the legal limits on prohibiting exports to foreign countries.
subfiles.summary: Moore acknowledges Cannon’s April 18 letter and expresses appreciation for thoughtful public comments. He explains that the Neutrality Act of 1939 does not provide the broad authority Cannon seeks and that, apart from laws concerning materials such as tinplate scrap and helium gas, the government lacks general power to prohibit exports of manufactured products or raw materials to a particular foreign country.

subfiles.title: Roger S. Greene forwards Ralph L. Harding’s embargo analysis
subfiles.about: Forwards an engineer’s detailed observations on the proposed embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Greene sends Hamilton a copy of a lengthy letter from Ralph L. Harding, an engineer who had lived in China, Japan, and the Philippines. He notes Harding’s former service as chief of the Commerce Department’s Metals and Minerals Division and says that Harding has studied the embargo question since 1931. Greene recommends the analysis as more informed than much of the committee’s other correspondence.

subfiles.title: Ralph L. Harding to Roger S. Greene on the case for an embargo against Japan
subfiles.about: Develops a moral, economic, and strategic case for immediately restricting exports of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Harding recalls that he favored an embargo after Japan entered Manchuria in 1931 but later doubted that it could work without British and European cooperation. Changed world conditions now lead him to conclude that Japan depends directly on the United States for scrap, metals, petroleum products, machinery, and other materials needed for its war in China. He argues that continued American trade supports atrocities, strengthens a future commercial and military rival, threatens access to Asian raw materials, and increases U.S. defense costs. Harding advocates immediate restrictions, government purchase and storage of exportable surpluses, support for synthetic substitutes for silk, and wider public education about the issue.
